column2: The sheets are driven or vibrated in before excavation; the soil face is never left unsupported, not even for a moment.
In fine sand, above what depth must it always be shored?
Fine sand 0,5 m, intermediate soil 1,0 m, hard clay 2,0 m – for occupational safety, because of drying and soaking.
What is the role of the waling in the shoring?
It holds the planks together and passes their load to the struts
As a compression member it braces the two soil faces against each other
It protects the ends of the planks from splitting
It drains the groundwater from behind the planks
Plank → waling → strut → opposite side: this is the load path of cross-bracing.
What strut pressure do we use for medium- and high-plasticity soil?
The greater of p₁ = (Hγn + q) − 4c and p₂ = 0,2·(Hγn + q)
The K·tan² formula applies to granular and low-plasticity (Ip < 10%) soils.
From the bottom up, keeping pace with backfilling in layers
From the top down, so that the workers can get out
All at once, lifted out by crane
First the planks are pulled out, then the struts
A strut may only come out once compacted backfill already supports the face below it.
When sinking trench boxes while digging, how far below the edge of the panel may they dig at most?
Any distance, if the soil is cohesive
Then the excavator pushes the box down corner by corner with the back of its bucket (the tilt of the struts at most 1:20).
Why is it difficult to brace an excavation wider than about 3 m with horizontal struts?
Because the earth pressure grows in proportion to the width
Because the excavator does not fit
The critical force decreases with the square of the strut length (N_cr ∝ 1/L²).
If the length of the strut doubles, the critical (Euler) force…
N_cr = π²EI/L² – that is why intermediate bracing or a larger cross-section is needed.
What has to be checked separately for raking struts?
The vertical equilibrium: the strut can rotate out, so it has to be flat enough
Only the tensile strength of the strut
The thermal expansion of the strut
Nothing, a raking strut is always stable
The vertical component of the force in the raking strut lifts the wall and pushes the foot down.
When can the shoring of a wide excavation be removed?
When the basement walls and slabs are complete and take the earth pressure as diaphragms
Right after the base slab is concreted
Until then the temporary support carries the earth pressure.
In a passive tieback, what is the wall tied to?
To I or U sections driven outside the failure plane, with steel bars running 0,8–1,0 m below the surface
To a thrust block built on the bottom of the excavation
To the opposite wall, with a tubular strut
The tie rods run in a narrow trench; this needs room beside the excavation.
Steel I-beams every 1–3 m (usually 2 m); between them, keeping pace with the excavation, horizontal planks wedged against the flanges. Load path: plank → soldier → support or embedment.
Intersecting jet columns (Ø 60–120 cm, spacing: D − 10–20 cm); a steel member fits only within 15–20 cm of the drilling axis. No lagging and no subsequent bore filling is needed.

A trench excavated by grab under slurry, like a diaphragm wall; instead of concrete, the cement-bearing slurry itself hardens. By arching, the slurry transfers the earth and water pressure to the beams.
Soil-cement mixed in place by wet deep mixing (e.g. CSM: panels 2,4–2,8 m × 0,55–1,2 m); steel I/H sections are set into the fresh mix.
A continuous wall of U (Larssen) or Z (Hoesch) steel piles threaded together by interlocks. As a temporary wall it can be fully extracted and reused.
Piles with gaps of 20–60 cm (at most D); the soil arches between them, and the face is protected from running by mesh + shotcrete. This is the most widespread in Hungary.
If the soil is not stable on its own (granular soil) but no watertightness is needed, or a close spacing is needed structurally.
First the unreinforced primary piles, then between them, cutting about 10–12 cm into them, the reinforced secondary piles. Only every second one is reinforced.
Panels excavated by grab under slurry, reinforced and concreted: a stiff, watertight wall, often part of the permanent structure.
